briefing.text: The last door. A keyword doorman out front, a vault bolted behind it. Talk past the doorman, then throw the bolt in the same breath. This is the score.

objectives.goal: Slip the blocked phrase past the doorman and lift the vault's door key.
objectives.why: The vault's ACL id isn't on any sign — the ledger is the only place it's written down.
objectives.doneWhen: The vault door's ACL id walks past the filter into the results.
objectives.approach: A guard out front rejects the obvious attack words. The move underneath is the same ledger-read you already know — you just have to disguise the banned words so the guard waves them through while the database still reads them as the command.

query.template: SELECT title, body FROM notices WHERE title LIKE '%{{input:q}}%'
query.description: Archive search, fronted by a keyword blocklist

inputFilter.message: ⛔ blocked: that phrase is on the doorman's list.

winCondition.reason: The phrase walked past the doorman and the vault's door id surfaced from the ledger.

hints.text: You already know the move from the Vault - a two-column pull from the ledger. The only new problem is the man at the door blocking the phrase. Don't invent a new attack. Disguise the old one.

The doorman matches the phrase letter-for-letter, so break it up with something SQLite treats as blank space. An inline comment /**/ between the two words does exactly that: the filter sees a different string, the database sees the keyword.

The blocked  ' UNION SELECT schematic, loot FROM archive_ledger --  becomes  ' UNION/**/SELECT schematic, loot FROM archive_ledger --  . Same query underneath; the /**/ splits the banned phrase so the filter never matches it.

expectedSolution.note: The naive ' UNION SELECT ... is rejected by the blocklist. Splitting UNION SELECT with an inline comment (/**/ = whitespace to SQLite) slips past the literal match while still parsing as UNION SELECT, and the ledger loot surfaces.

debrief.explanation: The doorman is a blocklist: it scans your raw input for literal phrases like 'UNION SELECT' and rejects the request if it finds one. But it's matching TEXT, while SQLite parses TOKENS. An inline comment /**/ is just characters to the filter - enough to break the phrase 'UNION SELECT' so the substring check misses - yet to SQLite a comment is whitespace, so 'UNION/**/SELECT' parses as the very keyword the filter meant to stop. Blocklists are brittle by nature: comments, extra whitespace, case, and encodings all route around them, and the query underneath is still built by concatenation.

vulnerableCodeVariants.label: Node.js (pg / mysql2)
Python (sqlite3 / psycopg2)
vulnerableCodeVariants.code:
# VULNERABLE - keyword blocklist bolted in front of a still-interpolated query
if re.search(r"union\s+(all\s+)?select", q, re.I):
    raise PermissionError("blocked")
cur.execute(f"SELECT title, body FROM notices WHERE title LIKE '%{q}%'")
rows = cur.fetchall()
# 'UNION/**/SELECT' never matches the regex; psycopg2 %-format is the same flaw

secureCodeVariants.label: Node.js (pg / mysql2)
Python (sqlite3 / psycopg2)
secureCodeVariants.code:
# SECURE - bind the LIKE pattern; the injection never forms, so there is nothing to filter
cur.execute(
    "SELECT title, body FROM notices WHERE title LIKE ?",
    ("%" + q + "%",),
)
rows = cur.fetchall()
# A WAF / keyword blocklist is defense-in-depth, NEVER the fix. Parameterize first;
# prefer an allowlist (what input is permitted) over a blocklist (guessing every bad word).
# psycopg2 uses %s: cur.execute("... title LIKE %s", ("%" + q + "%",))

debrief.takeaway: A list of forbidden words is just a list of words the attacker hasn't disguised yet. A WAF is not a fix - bind the query and the phrase stops mattering.

payoff.fixer: There's the vault's ACL id — VLT-DOOR-3E9A. Now flip its bolt in one breath.

objectives.goal: Stack a write onto the badge read and flip the vault's ACL to OPEN.
objectives.why: You lifted the door's id from the ledger — now force its grant to 1 in the same breath as a badge read.
objectives.doneWhen: An extra result set proves the stacked write hit VLT-DOOR-3E9A — the bolt flipped.
objectives.approach: You lifted the vault door's id from the ledger. This badge desk runs whatever you feed it, start to finish — so tack a SECOND command onto the badge lookup that flips that door's access to open, then read it back to prove the bolt moved.

query.template: SELECT door, granted FROM door_acl WHERE badge = '{{input:badge}}'
query.description: Badge access lookup (the whole input string is executed as a batch)

winCondition.reason: A second statement rode in behind the badge read — the vault door (VLT-DOOR-3E9A) flipped to granted and the verify read proved it.

hints.text: This desk doesn't just read your badge - it runs whatever you hand it, top to bottom. A single lookup is polite. Nothing's stopping you from being impolite and handing it a second instruction.

Close the quote, end the read with a semicolon, then write your own statement: UPDATE door_acl to set granted = 1 on the door id you lifted (VLT-DOOR-3E9A). Add one more SELECT so the change shows up as a result, and finish with -- to comment out the trailing quote.

In the badge box:  B-1001'; UPDATE door_acl SET granted = 1 WHERE door = 'VLT-DOOR-3E9A'; SELECT door, granted FROM door_acl WHERE door = 'VLT-DOOR-3E9A' --   The UPDATE is the break-in; the final SELECT is your receipt.

inputs.badge: B-1001'; UPDATE door_acl SET granted = 1 WHERE door = 'VLT-DOOR-3E9A'; SELECT door, granted FROM door_acl WHERE door = 'VLT-DOOR-3E9A' --

expectedSolution.note: The read must hit a real badge (B-1001) so its result set counts; then the stacked UPDATE flips the door id you lifted in the previous objective, and the final SELECT is the receipt.

debrief.explanation: Two failures again: your badge is concatenated into the SQL, and the desk runs the whole string as a batch — so a semicolon ends the app's read and starts a statement of your own. After 'B-1001' you close the quote, add ; UPDATE door_acl SET granted = 1 WHERE door = 'VLT-DOOR-3E9A' (the real damage — that id came from the ledger you lifted), then a second SELECT to verify, and -- to swallow the leftover quote. SQLite executes all of it in order: the harmless read, your write, and the confirming read. The extra result set is the proof the stacked statement ran.

Python (sqlite3 / psycopg2)
vulnerableCodeVariants.code:
# VULNERABLE - executescript() runs the WHOLE string as a batch of statements
sql = f"SELECT door, granted FROM door_acl WHERE badge = '{badge}'"
cur.executescript(sql)
# The stacked "; UPDATE door_acl SET granted=1 WHERE door='VAULT'" rides in as its own statement.
# psycopg2: one execute() with ';'-separated text runs the batch too.

secureCodeVariants.label: Node.js (pg / mysql2)
Python (sqlite3 / psycopg2)
secureCodeVariants.code:
# SECURE - execute() runs a SINGLE statement and binds the value
cur.execute("SELECT door, granted FROM door_acl WHERE badge = ?", (badge,))
rows = cur.fetchall()
# The ';'-payload becomes an inert string; executescript() is the footgun to avoid.
# psycopg2: cur.execute("... badge = %s", (badge,)) is single-statement too.

debrief.takeaway: A question should ask one thing. Bind the value AND let the driver run a single statement - so a semicolon is a syntax error, not a to-do list.

payoff.fixer: Two moves, one breath — the vault's ACL flipped to OPEN. That's the job.
